Chapter 3History

p. 60

Prop and Wings

The Prop and Wings (propeller and wings) is a military insignia used to identify various aviation-related units in the United States military. The Prop and Wings originated as branch insignia of the United States Army Air Service in 1920, and remained such from 1926 to 1947 for the successor United States Army Air Corps. It is now worn after successful completion of program requirements. The Prop & Wings is the symbol of the American Airman. First worn by Aviation Cadets in 1917, the tradition continued in other commissioning programs. The Prop & Wings symbol is now worn by all Air Force Academy, Reserve Officer Training Corps (ROTC) cadets, and Officer Training School (OTS) trainees who have met the challenges of the first phase of officer training. Through completion of this common experience, they have earned the right to be accepted as full members of the Long Blue Line of the U.S. Air Force. As future leaders of the Air Force, all graduates of OTS and ROTC lay their hands on this historic plaque. Descendants of Air Force, Army Air Corps, or WASP members are authorized gold.

Inscription:

Established here in 1931, was the birthplace and nurturing ground of American air doctrine. In the ferment of a decade of thought and debate, the Air Corps Tactical School gave rise to concepts for the strategic and operational deployment of U.S. air power against two formidable aggressor nations separated by half a world. Validation of this revolutionary approach to warfare came with victory over the Axis with fewer casualties than in advancing a few hundred miles in World War I.

Most of America's senior air officers of World War II – including the legendary Claire Chennault, Ira Eaker, Harold George, Haywood S . Hansell, Laurence Kuter and Curtis LeMay – were instructors or graduates of the school. This memorial honors their visionary achievements and stands in tribute to the intellectual energy which fashioned the air power concepts so crucial to victory.

p. 61

Air University, born of the Air Corps Tactical School, continues the legacy – generating ideas needed for the rapid advance of the air and space power so vital to our nation and its future.

Erected in 1994 by the Citizens of Montgomery and the Montgomery Chapter of the Air Force Association.

Photographs By Mark Hilton, November 22, 2014

p. 62

History of Air Force Reserve Officers’ Training Corps Air Force Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (AFROTC) is the largest and oldest source of commissioned officers for the Air Force. AFROTC is designed to recruit, educate, and commission officer candidates through academic education, Field Training and Officer Development programs based on Air Force and Space Force requirements. Students can attend classes through host or cross-town enrollment programs. Cadet enrollments have ranged from a high of 23,605 in 1986 to a low of 10,231 in 1993. AFROTC was established with the passage of the National Defense Act of 1916, which established program guidelines that remained in effect until 1964. The Army Reorganization Act of 1920 created ROTC units specifically designed to train rated officers for the Air Corps. By 1926, seven such units existed, but a lack of funds to support flight training forced three to close in 1928 and the remainder units only trained non-rated officers. Since the Air Corps had virtually no requirement for non- rated officers, it closed the remaining units in 1933.

After World War II, Gen Dwight D. Eisenhower, Chief of Staff of the War Department, signed General Order No. 124, establishing AFROTC units at 78 colleges and universities throughout the nation. Eligible Air Force enlisted men and women pursuing a college degree who were interested in becoming commissioned officers were given that opportunity through competition in the AFROTC Airman Scholarship and Commissioning Program, established in 1973.

In 1978, Air Training Command (ATC) assumed responsibility for AFROTC programs. On 1 July 1993, ATC merged with Air University to form Air Education and Training Command. Air University became a direct reporting unit under Air Education and Training Command and AFROTC realigned under Air Force Accessions Center. In February 1997, AFROTC and Officer Training School merged under the newly created parent organization, HQ Air Force Officer Accession and Training Schools (AFOATS). This restructuring placed oversight for three-quarters of Air Force officer production under one command and facilitated the sharing of manpower and expertise with minimum effect on the day-to-day operations of either organization. In June 2008, HQ AFOATS was re-designated as the Jeanne M. Holm Center for Officer Accessions and Citizen Development. In 2020, USSF officers began commissioning through the AFROTC program. The Air Force Accession Center activated on 1 Dec, 2024 and consolidates the Holm Center and AFROTC.

Air and Space Leaders

p. 63

The following Airmen are representative of the whose exceptional contributions shaped and influenced our Air Force and continue to inspire today’s Airmen. “Air power is indivisible. If you split it up into compartments, you merely pull it to pieces and destroy its greatest asset— its flexibility.”

- Field Marshal Viscount Bernard L. Montgomery General Curtis E. LeMay General LeMay started his career as a cadet in the Army Air Corps flying school in 1928 after graduating from the ROTC program at Ohio State University. On 12 May 1938, LeMay led three B-17’s on a mission to intercept the Italian liner Rex. With this success, LeMay confirmed air power had the potential for defending our nation from sea attack as well as affirming the navigational capabilities of long-range bombers. Regarded as one of the greatest combat commanders in Air Force history, LeMay led the Schweinfurt-Regensburg raid of 1943 and commanded the 20th and 21st Bomber Commands in 1945. Over the years, LeMay earned the reputation as an extraordinary pilot and navigator. “We will always need manned systems—manned planes, manned spacecraft. Missiles are spectacular and they play their role, but they have no sense of loyalty; they can’t think; they can’t be recalled.” LeMay continued to lead by example and became Commander of the United States Air Forces in Europe (USAFE from 1947– 1948, Commander-in-Chief, Strategic Air Command from 1948–1957, and USAF Chief of Staff from 1961–1965.

General James H. “Jimmy” Doolittle

General Doolittle enlisted in the Army Signal Corps Reserve in October 1917 as a flying cadet. Doolittle resigned from the Army Air Corps in 1930; but ten years later in July 1940, he returned to active duty. In April of 1942, he led 16 B-25 medium bombers on the first American bombing attack against the homeland of Japan from the deck of the USS Hornet. As a result of this bombing run on Tokyo, he received the Medal of Honor. In his career, he was the commander of the Twelfth Air Force in North Africa, the Fifteenth Air Force in Italy, and the Eighth Air Force in England. Doolittle advocated the creation of an independent Air Force. “The first lesson is that you cannot lose a war if you have command of the air and you cannot win a war if you haven’t.” Doolittle, nicknamed the “Renaissance Man of Aviation,” was a test pilot as well as a daredevil and risk taker who made deliberate decisions. Doolittle died in California on 27 September 1993.

Brigadier General William “Billy” Mitchell

Brig General Mitchell was a prominent crusader for air power. His career started when he became a second lieutenant in the volunteer signal company. Mitchell became the driving force for advocating the strength and power that aeronautics would play in the future as an equal partner to the Army and Navy. He proposed the Department of Aeronautics should be in charge of the training and personnel used by the other services. Mitchell proposed that the airplane was superior to the battleship, which he tried to demonstrate by sinking the Ostfriesland on 22 July 1921. In many ways, his ideas and methods sparked controversy and disapproval, which led to his

p. 64

court-martial. Mitchell attempted to gain support with his first book, Our Air Force. Mitchell contributed to the doctrinal and tactical growth of the Air Service despite the opposition that he struggled against.

General Carl. A “Tooey” Spaatz

General Spaatz graduated from West Point in 1914. He began flight training in 1915 at Rockwell Field, San Diego. “Tooey” was a man of few words but always in control. He brought public attention to the Army Air Service as commander of the Far West Flying Circus putting on stunting and dogfighting exhibitions. General Carl Spaatz was named by President Truman as the first Chief of Staff of the Air Force on 25 Sep 1947 and was sworn in on 26 Sep 1947. Spaatz, like Eaker, realized the importance of a separate Air Force. His commands included Commander of the Eighth Air Force, Commander of the North African Air Force, and Commander of U.S. Strategic Air Forces in Europe. "Spaatz was mission commander for the 'Question Mark’ crew that flew for 150 hours, 40 minutes, and 15 seconds on 7 January 1929.

General Ira C. Eaker

General Eaker began his flying career in 1918 when he was placed on detached service to receive flying instruction at Austin and Kelly fields in Texas. Eaker understood the necessity of popular support in order for air power to be established once the U.S. began arming for the war in Europe in 1938. Eaker was a primary USAAF representative establishing the British–U.S. combined bomber offensive of WWII, and he led bombing raids on German-occupied Europe as commander of the Eighth Air Force.

General Bernard A. Schriever

General Schriever was what many consider to be the Founding Father of the U.S. Space program. He followed the Army Air Corps to what is now the U.S. Air Force. Schriever is credited for overcoming the technical challenges that presented themselves during the development of the ICBM. His tremendous effort to get the missiles developed and deployed, especially in the light of the space race that began as a result of his efforts, directly affected America’s ability to compete for control of space. His tremendous achievements were reflected and rewarded by the redesignation of Falcon AFB in Colorado Springs to Schriever AFB in 1998 and later Schriever Space Force Base in 2021.

p. 65

First Lieutenant Karl W. Richter

First Lt. Karl Richter's story is one of remarkable courage and perseverance. An Air Force Academy graduate, Richter flew F-105Ds in the 421st TFS, 388th TFW, Korat RTAFB. He flew aggressively and volunteered for the most hazardous missions. In September 1966, he shot down a MiG-17. As he neared the end of his 100-mission tour, Richter asked for and received permission to fly 100 more missions back-to-back. On his second tour, he was awarded an Air Force Cross for a mission on April 20, 1967, in which he vigorously suppressed heavy AAA and SAM defenses. In July 1967, on his 198th mission, Lt. Richter was hit by enemy fire and ejected over sharp limestone rocks known as karst. He was mortally injured when he hit the rocks.

Captain Lance P. Sijan

Captain Lance P. Sijan was an American Air Force pilot during the Vietnam War. Born in 1942, he grew up in a patriotic family and graduated the Air Force Academy in 1965. Sijan was assigned to the 480th Tactical Fighter Squadron in Vietnam. On November 9, 1967, Sijan's aircraft was hit by enemy fire, and he ejected but was severely injured. Despite his injuries, he survived for 46 days in the Vietnamese jungle, evading capture. Sijan endured starvation, dehydration, and infections before being captured on Christmas Day. Throughout his captivity, he never divulged sensitive information to his captors.

Sijan's health rapidly declined, but he continued to resist his captors and inspire fellow POWs. Tragically, he died on January 22, 1968, at the age of 25. Sijan’ remarkable bravery and commitment earned him numerous accolades. In 1976, Sijan posthumously received the Medal of Honor, the highest US military decoration. He was the first Air Force Academy graduate to receive this honor. Lance Sijan's story remains an inspiration to military personnel. His unwavering courage and resilience in the face of adversity have solidified his status as a true American hero.

p. 66

Air and Space Force Events

March 16, 1926 - Dr. Robert H. Goddard launched the first liquid fueled rocket in history. It flew 184 feet and started the age of Modern Rocketry.

April 12, 1981 - The first Space Shuttle Orbiter, OV-102 Columbia, manned by John Young (commander) and Robert Crippen (pilot) was successfully launched by NASA from Cape Canaveral.

April 18, 1942 - Led by Lt Colonel James H. Doolittle, 16 B-25s took off from the carrier USS Hornet in the first raid on Tokyo.

Although all 16 planes were lost, 14 crews came through alive. Lt Colonel Doolittle was awarded the Medal of Honor, and the other flyers received the Distinguished Flying Cross.

May 5, 1961 - Commander Alan B. Shepard, Jr., USN, became the first U.S. astronaut to enter space. His Project Mercury capsule, “Freedom 7,’’ was boosted from Cape Canaveral, Florida, by a Mercury Redstone (MR-3) rocket to a height of 115 miles. The flight lasted 15 min 28 sec, traveled 302 miles, and reached a maximum speed of 5,000 mph.

May 12, 1949 - The Soviet blockade of Berlin was lifted, ending the Berlin Airlift and signifying a great moral victory for the Western Powers. During the 462 days of “Operation Vittles’’ that preceded the end of the airlift on September 30, 1949, U.S. planes had officially carried 1,783,826 tons of supplies in 277,262 flights. The airlift demonstrated the importance of air power as an instrument of national policy.

June 3–7, 1965 - During the 4-day flight of the Gemini 4 capsule, Major Edward H. White, USAF, was the first American to walk in space. Major James A. McDivitt, USAF, was the mission commander. Astronaut White spent 22 minutes outside the capsule, connected by a 25-foot tether and oxygen cord. June 27, 1923 - Lt Lowell H. Smith and Lt John P. Richter, flying a DH-4 together with Lt Virgil Hine and Lt Frank W. Seifert performed the first pipeline aerial refueling over San Diego, California.

July 20, 1969 - Fulfilling President Kennedy’s statement of national objective, the U.S. landed the first manned space vehicle on the moon at 4:17:41 (EDT. The Lunar Module, named Eagle, carried NASA Commander Neil A.

Armstrong and LM pilot Colonel Edwin E. Aldrin, Jr., USAF, to the surface while Lt Colonel Michael Collins, USAF, orbited in the Command and Service Module, named Columbia. At 10:56:20 (EDT Astronaut Armstrong became the first man to step on the moon.

July 26, 1947 - The National Security Act became law. The law provided for the establishment of the third military department, the Air Force, and the National Military Establishment, headed by a civilian Secretary of War, for unified direction of the Services.

p. 67

August 6, 1945 - The first atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima, Japan. The bomb, nicknamed “Little Boy,’’ was delivered by the B-29 “Enola Gay,” under the command of Colonel Paul W. Tibbets, Jr.

August 29, 2019 - United States Space Command was re-established, becoming the 11th Combatant Command which reemphasized focus on space as a warfighting domain. September 1, 1975 - One of the original Tuskegee Airmen, Daniel “Chappie’’ James pinned on his fourth star and became commander of North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD). General James became the first African-American officer to achieve the rank of four-star general.

September 18, 1947 - The initiation of Executive Order 9877 defined the roles and mission of the Air Force. Although the National Security Act was passed on July 26, its effective date was September 18 when W. Stuart Symington was sworn in as the first Secretary of the Air Force. On September 26, General Carl A. Spaatz was sworn in as the first Air Force Chief of Staff.

September 28, 1924 - Completion of the first around-the world flight in aviation history. Four Douglas biplanes, under the command of Major Frederick L. Martin, left on the 26,350-mile journey on April 6. After 175 days, 363 hours flying time, two planes returned under command of Lieutenant Lowell H. Smith. October 2, 1942 - The first jet flight by an American aircraft. The plane was the XP-59A built by Bell Aircraft Corporation with two General Electric I-1A turbojets mounted beneath the wings close to the fuselage. During its first flight of 30 minutes, the plane approached 400 mph.

October 14, 1947 - On this date, the Bell X-1 became the first piloted plane to break the speed of sound. It was launched from a B-29. With Captain Charles E. Yeager as pilot, the plane reached a height of approx. 43,000 feet in 2 minutes and 30 seconds of powered flight. Captain Yeager named the plane Glamorous Glennis after his wife.

November 8, 1950 - First all jet aerial combat in history. Lieutenant Russell J. Brown in an F-80 shot down a Russian MiG-15 over North Korea.

December 17, 1903 - The Wright brothers, Orville and Wilbur, made the first sustained, controlled, powered flights from Kill Devil Hill, Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The fourth and longest flight covered a distance of 852 feet in 59 seconds. Three days earlier, on the 14th they had made the first powered flight lasting 3.5 seconds for a distance of 105 feet.

December 20, 2019 - The 2020 National Defense Authorization Act was signed into law establishing the Space Force as the sixth armed service branch under the Department of the Air Force. On January 14, 2020, General John “Jay”

Raymond was sworn in as the first Chief of Space Operations.

p. 68

United States Air Force Heritage The Wright Brothers Drawing upon a systematic study of aeronautical literature, practical experience from their bicycle shop, and supreme confidence, Orville and Wilbur Wright developed the first successful heavier-than-air, powered aircraft. With the assistance of American glider pioneer Octave Chanute, the Wrights made over a thousand glider flights from Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina from 1900 to 1902, perfecting wing warping, elevators, rudders, and a small four- cylinder engine.

On December 14, 1903, they attempted the first flight of a powered aircraft. Stalling the aircraft upon take off and crashing three seconds later. At 10:35 on December 17, 1903, Orville Wright made the first flight of 120 feet in 12 seconds. Alternating pilot duties, the brothers flew three more flights with Wilbur flying 852 feet and staying aloft 59 seconds on their fourth attempt. By 1905, Wright Flyer No. 3 constituted the first practical airplane with one flight lasting 39 minutes and covering 24 miles.

The Introduction of Military Air Power

On Aug 1, 1907, the U.S. Army established an Aeronautical Division within the Signal Corps. By Dec 1907, the Division established specs for bidding on a military aircraft. The Wright brothers submitted a flyable aircraft, the Wright Type A Military Flyer. In September 1908, the Flyer carried the first military observer, but crashed, resulting in one death and injuries to Orville Wright. Nonetheless, the Army accepted the plane as the first in its inventory in August 1909. In October 1909, Wilbur Wright trained two pilots, who later crashed the plane. Lt Benjamin Foulois became the Signal Corps' chief pilot in March 1910. By October 1912, the Aeronautical Division had 11 aircraft and 14 flying officers. In July 1914, the Aviation Section within the Signal Corps was established with 60 officers and 260 enlisted men. In March 1916, the Army's 1st Aero Squadron joined the Punitive Expedition in Mexico, but all eight aircraft were destroyed by the end of April.

World War I, The First Expeditionary Air Force

Less than eight months after the Punitive Expedition, the US entered WWI. The Signal Corps Aviation Section had officers, enlisted men, and airplanes. Aircraft evolved from observation craft to weapons of war, with observation, artillery spotting, and reconnaissance being their main contributions. Pursuit aircraft sought control of the skies, with French pilot Roland Garros attaching steel plates to his plane's propeller to fire a machine gun. The Germans created the Fokker Eindecker, the first true fighter plane. The "Fokker scourge” threatened Allied forces until they developed their own interrupter gear. The Escadrille Américaine, later renamed Lafayette Escadrille, was established for American volunteers. Pilots such as Raoul Lufbery, Edward Rickenbacker, and Frank Luke gained fame. Colonel William Mitchell became the outstanding air combat commander. Mitchell emphasized mass attacks during the St. Mihiel offensive, which contributed to the Allied victory. The Air Service grew exponentially during the war, with 195,024 personnel and 7,900 aircraft by the end. Gen Billy Mitchell, the Ostfriesland and the Inter-War Air Corps

p. 69

After World War I, two themes emerged in American air power: Billy Mitchell's push for Air Force independence and a focus on aviation records. Mitchell believed in the potential of air power as a revolutionary weapon and challenged the Navy's battleships by sinking the Ostfriesland and two other ships with bombers. Although he failed to convince the War or Navy Departments, the bombing tests led to the development of carrier-based aviation. Mitchell's frustration led to public statements and a court martial, resulting in a five-year suspension. He resigned to continue fighting for an independent Air Force. The Air Corps Act of 1926 improved aviation's status in the Army, transforming the Air Service into the Air Corps. Throughout the next decade, the Air Corps made advancements in delivering mail, coastal defense, and instrument flying. In 1935, all air combat units were organized into the General Headquarters (GHQ) Air Force.

WWII, The Doolittle Raid

In 1939, the GHQ Air Force began an expansion program that would become the largest air organization in history. President Roosevelt requested $300 million for military aviation. The Air Corps planned for 24 combat-ready groups by 1941, requiring more manpower, training, and equipment. On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the US Pacific fleet at Pearl Harbor, causing significant damage. President Roosevelt wanted to boost morale with an offensive strike against Japan. Navy Captain Low suggested using Army bombers from a Navy carrier. The B-25 was chosen for its size and capabilities. Modifications were made to the bombers to increase their effectiveness. On April 18, 1942, Lt Col James Doolittle led a successful raid on Tokyo, Kobe, and Nagoya. Although the raid caused minimal damage, it shocked Japanese leaders and boosted American morale. Doolittle received the Medal of Honor and a promotion to Brigadier General.

Air Corps Innovation in the Pacific

George C. Kenney was a pioneering airman whose career spanned both World Wars. After enlisting in the Aviation Section of the U.S. Signal Corps in 1917, he served with the 91st Aero Squadron in France during World War I. During the interwar years, Kenney attended the Air Corps Tactical School and the Army War College, while also contributing to aviation development by refining techniques for mounting machine guns on aircraft wings and experimenting with low-level attack tactics. In 1940, as Assistant Air Attaché in France, he observed German and Allied air operations and recommended improvements to U.S. aircraft and combat tactics. His expertise led to senior assignments at Wright Field and promotion to brigadier general in 1941. In July 1942, General Douglas MacArthur selected Kenney to command Allied Air Forces and the Fifth Air Force in the Southwest Pacific. There, Kenney pioneered innovative tactics such as low-level attacks, skip bombing, parafrag weapons, and the modification of B-25 bombers into heavily armed anti-shipping aircraft. These innovations contributed significantly to the Allied victory in the Battle of the Bismarck Sea in 1943. Later commanding the Far East Air Forces, which included the Fifth, Thirteenth, and Seventh Air Forces, Kenney demonstrated the decisive impact of adaptive airpower on the Pacific War and became one of the most influential air commanders in U.S. military history. Over Hitler’s Europe with “The Mighty Eighth”

p. 70

The Air Corps Tactical School (ACTS) played a crucial role in the development of air warfare doctrine, focusing on strategic bombardment and the use of heavy bombers. The theory, known as the "industrial web" or HAPDB, emphasized the destruction of enemy vital centers to collapse their economy and will to fight. The B-17 "Flying Fortress" and the Norden bombsight were seen as the perfect combination to fulfill this doctrine. The Eighth Air Force, based in England, became the symbol of the American air war against Germany. Their first operational bombing mission in August 1942 showed promise, even though it faced significant challenges. However, a mission in October 1943 against Schweinfurt resulted in severe losses for the Eighth Air Force, leading to a change in strategy.

The introduction of the P-51 Mustang revolutionized the air war over Europe. Its superior speed, maneuverability, and range allowed it to outperform German fighters. With the support of both the Eighth and Fifteenth Air Forces, Operation ARGUMENT, also known as "Big Week," aimed to achieve air superiority and cripple Germany's aircraft industry. The operation, conducted in February 1944, successfully destroyed a significant number of German fighters and turned the tide in favor of the U.S. Strategic Air Force. By June 1944, allied air forces dominated the skies over Europe during the D-Day invasion. The Luftwaffe was unable to mount a significant defense, with only a handful of sorties and minimal damage inflicted on the invasion beaches.

Overall, the development of air power doctrine, the use of heavy bombers, and the introduction of superior aircraft like the P-51 Mustang played a crucial role in achieving air superiority and contributing to the success of the Allied forces in World War II.

An Emerging Tactical Support Mission

American Airmen, led by Major Elwood "Pete" Quesada, pioneered the concept of close air support even before the Allies invaded Europe. Inspired by the Royal Air Force's efforts, Quesada moved beyond the strategic bombing doctrine taught at the Air Corps Tactical School. During the invasion of Italy, fighter aircraft proved their value in close air support missions, flying over sixty percent of them. The P-47 Thunderbolt, with field modifications made by Airmen on the ground, became the most effective tactical air support platform of the war.

Under Quesada's command, the Ninth Fighter Command enhanced communication between planes and ground troops. Air Support Parties, equipped with radios and colored ground panels, helped minimize friendly-fire incidents. However, the use of B-17s in a tactical role resulted in tragic consequences during Operation COBRA, claiming the life of Lieutenant General Leslie McNair.

Despite this setback, tactical air support continued to evolve and improve throughout the war. Pilots embedded in armored columns communicated with planes to provide cover and support during the Normandy breakout. The Nineteenth Tactical Air Command, led by General Otto P. Weyland, effectively guarded General George Patton's flanks during his rapid advance across Southern France.

p. 71

By the end of the war, communication and effectiveness in tactical air support had significantly improved. The efforts of Airmen on the ground and in the air played a crucial role in supporting ground troops and ensuring their success against the enemy.

General Benjamin O. Davis, Jr. And The Tuskegee Airmen

The Tuskegee Airmen, led by General Benjamin O. Davis, Jr., played a significant role in changing racial attitudes in the military during World War II. Despite facing institutional racism and segregation, they demonstrated resilience and valor in combat. The creation of a separate flight school for black aviation candidates at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama paved the way for blacks to be trained for the Army Air Force service.

Under the leadership of Captain Benjamin O. Davis, Jr., the 99th Pursuit Squadron became the first-ever black combat unit in the Air Corps. They trained tirelessly, facing racism and poor command support. In April 1943, the squadron received orders to the Mediterranean Theatre of Operations, where they provided air support to ground troops. Despite being segregated and receiving little training or supplies, they flew numerous missions, including escorting bombers and engaging in combat with Nazi fighters.

Colonel Davis later assumed command of the all-black 332d Fighter Group, rebuilding morale, which included the 99th Fighter Squadron. The 332d Fighter Group, known as the "Red Tails" due to their distinctive aircraft markings, excelled in bomber escort missions. They developed effective tactics, such as the "Top Cover" tactic, to protect bombers from Nazi fighters.

Throughout the war, the Tuskegee Airmen demonstrated exceptional skill and professionalism, earning praise and respect from bomber crews. They shot down enemy aircraft, destroyed ground targets, and saved the lives of countless bomber crews. The Tuskegee Program became a model for the integration of the United States Air Force, with officers and enlisted personnel from diverse backgrounds working together.

After the war, Colonel Davis continued to make significant contributions to the Air Force. He led the 332d Fighter Group to victory in the first USAF Gunnery Meet, and later played a key role in the creation of the Thunderbirds precision flying team. General Benjamin O. Davis, Jr.'s achievements as a leader, officer, and aviator are a testament to his strength and determination to serve his nation in the United States Air Force. His leadership, along with the bravery and skill of the Tuskegee Airmen, paved the way for racial integration in the military and inspired future generations.

The WASPs

The formation of the Women Airforce Service Pilots (WASPs) in 1943 marked a significant milestone in the increased opportunities for women in the Air Corps during World War II. The WASPs were formed by combining the Women's Auxiliary Ferrying Squadron (WAFS) and the Women's Flying Training Detachment (WFTD).

Jacqueline "Jackie" Cochran, a renowned aviator and businesswoman, played a crucial

p. 72

role in advocating for women pilots in the war effort. Cochran, who had already achieved numerous aviation records and accolades, convinced Eleanor Roosevelt to support the idea of employing women pilots. Cochran herself became the first female pilot to fly a bomber across the Atlantic.

Becoming a WASP was highly competitive, and applicants had to possess a pilot's license. Out of the 25,000 women who applied, only 1,830 were accepted, and just 1,074 successfully completed the training. Once accepted, the women learned to fly military aircraft. Between 1942 and 1944, the WASPs delivered over 12,650 aircraft of various types, making up more than half of the ferrying of combat aircraft within the United States during the war. Their contributions were vital to the war effort, but for many years, the WASPs were not considered military personnel.

It was not until 1977, after years of lobbying, that the WASPs were granted full military status for their service by President Jimmy Carter. In 1984, each WASP received the World War II Victory Medal in recognition of their contributions.

The establishment of the WASPs paved the way for greater opportunities for women in the United States Air Force. In 1969, Air Force ROTC opened to women, and in 1971, Jeanne M. Holm became the first woman in the Air Force to be promoted to brigadier general. Additionally, women were admitted for the first time to all U.S. service academies.

The Air War in China

After the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor, American volunteers in the Pacific sided with the Chinese in a war against Japan. The American Volunteer Group, also known as the "Flying Tigers," began attacking the Japanese with innovative tactics and destroyed 296 enemy aircraft. The AVG inspired American fliers and provided valuable combat experience and tactics. The group was disbanded in 1942, and Colonel Claire Lee Chennault was promoted to brigadier general and tasked with defending the aerial supply route between India and China. The Fourteenth Air Force and Tenth Air Force conducted operations in support of Chinese forces and achieved air superiority over China by the end of the war. They also destroyed significant resources and infrastructure belonging to the Japanese ground forces in the China-Burma-India theater.

Dropping the Atomic Bomb

The U.S. Army Air Forces, the predecessor to today's U.S. Air Force, played a central role in the final stages of World War II through the delivery of the atomic bombs on Japan. On August 6, 1945, a B-29 Superfortress bomber named Enola Gay dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima, followed by a second B-29, Bockscar, which dropped another atomic bomb on Nagasaki on August 9, 1945. These missions were conducted by specially trained aircrews of the 509th Composite Group and remain among the most significant and controversial operations in military history. The bombings, combined with other wartime factors, contributed to Japan's decision to surrender, leading to the end of World War II on September 2, 1945.

Creating the United States Air Force

p. 73

After World War II, the United States went through a transition from a wartime to a peacetime military. The air forces significantly reduced in size, with a decrease in aircraft and personnel. The USAAF was reorganized into three commands: the Strategic Air Command (SAC), which focused on delivering air power to distant lands; the continental Air Defense Command (ADC), which defended the U.S. homeland; and the Tactical Air Command (TAC), which initially had no planes or operational units. In 1947, President Truman signed the National Security Act, which established a separate Department of the Air Force. W. Stuart Symington became the first Secretary of the Air Force, and the United States Air Force became an independent branch of the military under the leadership of General Carl A. Spaatz.

The Berlin Airlift

The Berlin Airlift was a response to the Soviet blockade of West Berlin in 1948. The United States organized an airlift operation to provide food, medicine, and coal to the residents of West Berlin. The operation involved American and British aircraft flying supplies into the city. The airlift lasted for fifteen months and was successful in delivering over 2 million tons of supplies. It demonstrated the strategic capabilities of American airlift and its ability to influence conflicts without resorting to violence. The Soviets eventually lifted the blockade in 1949.

Space and the Planes

The X-planes were experimental aircraft and rockets used by the United States to test new technologies and aerodynamic concepts after World War II. They made significant advancements in aviation, including breaking the sound barrier and demonstrating supersonic travel. The X-5, X-18, X-19, and X-22 explored features like variable geometry wings and vertical take-off and landing, which are now used in aircraft like the F-111 Aardvark and V-22 Osprey. The X-22, X-23, and X-24 tested technologies that contributed to the development of the Space Shuttle. The X-15 program produced eight pilots who qualified as astronauts, with Major Robert M. White being the first to reach an altitude of fifty miles and fly at six times the speed of sound. The X-planes also produced astronauts who were not part of NASA's Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo programs. While some technologies from the X-planes were successfully integrated, others, like the nuclear-powered X-6 bomber, never flew.

The Strategic Air Command and The Cold War

The Strategic Air Command (SAC) was created in 1946 to manage the United States' nuclear weapons and delivery systems. It was established after the 1946 Berlin Crisis and the Soviet Union's atomic bomb test in 1949 highlighted the need for better war readiness. Under the leadership of General Curtis E. LeMay, SAC focused on rigorous training, high performance standards, and immediate readiness. They incorporated more powerful bombers like the B-50 and the Convair B-36 Peacemaker, which had intercontinental range. In the 1950s, they upgraded to all-jet bombers like the B-47 Stratojet, B-58 Hustler, and the iconic B-52 Stratofortress. SAC also conducted secret electronic reconnaissance and occasional covert overflights of Soviet territory to assess air defenses. They remained on continuous alert with nuclear-armed bombers ready for immediate action. SAC's capabilities expanded with the development of intermediate range missiles, intercontinental

p. 74

ballistic missiles, and cruise missiles. They also had advanced surveillance and reconnaissance aircraft like the U-2, SR-71, and early unmanned aerial vehicles. While SAC is best known for its role in preparing for and deterring nuclear war, it also achieved significant results in conventional combat.

The Korean War

During the initial phase of the Korean War, American Airmen faced challenges due to their lack of preparedness and outdated equipment. The limited range of F-80 jets hindered their ability to provide close air support and interdiction. However, FEAF Bomber Command B- 29s conducted strategic operations to weaken the enemy's fighting capabilities.

Although United Nations air forces achieved air superiority and destroyed North Korea's industrial base, they faced technological, political, and operational limitations that prevented a decisive victory. The entry of half a million Chinese troops and the appearance of advanced Soviet-made MiG-15 fighters changed the nature of the war.

The F-86 Sabre, a beloved and classic fighter, was rushed into action to counter the MiG-15. The F-86 proved to be equal in speed and a more stable gun platform than the MiG-15. In the battles over "MiG Alley," USAF pilots with superior training and experience achieved an alleged 10:1 kill ratio, with F-86 pilots destroying 792 MiGs and 18 other enemy aircraft.

Although the F-86 pilots did not match the kill counts of World War II aces, they established themselves as a new group of fighter aces. Captain Joseph C. McConnell and Captain James Jabara were among the top scorers, with 16 and 15 kills respectively. These pilots devised new tactics based on small flights of four F-86s, deviating from the mass squadron formations of World War II.

Despite the stalemate on the ground, Air Force pilots continued their successful heritage in air-to-air combat during the Korean War.

The Space Race

The launch of Sputnik I by the Soviets in 1957 showed their potential to launch nucleararmed missiles at the United States. In response, President Eisenhower approved the Corona program, a joint effort by the Air Force and CIA to develop reconnaissance satellites. The program faced challenges in getting the satellite over the Soviet Union, taking useful pictures, and transmitting them back to the US. It took two years and twelve failed attempts before Corona successfully launched a satellite in 1960. This marked the first US military operations in space. Many early astronauts, such as Cooper, Grissom, and Slayton, were former military pilots who made significant contributions to space exploration. Borman and Anders were part of Apollo 8, the first mission to orbit the moon, and Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11.

The Vietnam Conflict

The United States Air Force played a crucial role in the Vietnam War, with its operations

p. 75

spanning from the early stages of the conflict to its eventual conclusion. Operation FARMGATE, initiated in 1961, saw American pilots training the South Vietnamese Air Force, providing them with the necessary skills and support to combat growing Communist influence in the region. However, it was the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964 that triggered a significant escalation of American involvement.

In response to the alleged attacks on the USS Maddox and USS Turner Joy by North Vietnamese torpedo boats, President Lyndon B. Johnson authorized Operation BARREL ROLL and Operation ROLLING THUNDER. These operations aimed to target Communist forces in Laos and North Vietnam, respectively, and demonstrate American resolve to support South Vietnam. However, the United States underestimated the resilience and determination of the enemy.

Operation ROLLING THUNDER went down in history as one of the most ineffective air campaigns conducted by the USAF. It disregarded established air doctrine, had questionable targeting strategies, and suffered from high losses. The stringent rules of engagement imposed on American pilots negated the speed, surprise, and flexibility that massed air power could provide. Furthermore, periodic "bombing pauses" intended to signal diplomatic intentions allowed the enemy to recover and regroup. Recognizing the deteriorating political and military situation in South Vietnam, President Richard Nixon took office in 1969 and implemented a new strategy known as "Vietnamization." This policy aimed to gradually shift the burden of combat onto the South Vietnamese forces while reducing US troop presence. Nixon began a phased withdrawal of American troops, which saw their numbers dwindle from a peak of 536,000 in 1968 to less than 100,000 by 1972. However, the North Vietnamese launched the Easter Offensive in 1972, prompting Nixon to respond with Operation LINEBACKER. In contrast to the ineffective ROLLING THUNDER, Operation LINEBACKER saw Nixon significantly reduce the restrictions on war fighting. The introduction of new television-and laser-guided "smart" bombs greatly improved strike accuracy, enabling American aircraft to target previously elusive enemy positions. Notably, on May 13, 1972, sixteen F-4 Phantoms successfully destroyed the Than Hoa Bridge using these advanced munitions. Operation LINEBACKER also produced the first aces of the war, with Captain Steve Ritchie, Captain Charles DeBellevue, and Captain Jeffrey S. Feinstein achieving notable kills.

Despite the tactical successes of Operation LINEBACKER, the Vietnam War would ultimately end in a disappointing manner for the United States. In December 1972, North Vietnamese intransigence over the final peace agreement prompted President Nixon to authorize Operation LINEBACKER II, an intense 11-day air campaign aimed at pressuring enemy compliance. B-52 bombers conducted strikes near Hanoi for the first time, dropping thousands of tons of bombs. Though the campaign broke the impasse and led to the resumption of peace talks, it was not enough to prevent the ultimate fall of South Vietnam.

In April 1975, North Vietnamese forces overran Saigon, marking the end of the Vietnam War and the reunification of Vietnam under Communist rule. The extensive efforts made by the US Air Force, which included over five million sorties, eight million tons of bombs dropped, and the loss of 1,459 aircraft, could not prevent the

p. 76

ultimate outcome. The war highlighted the versatility and wide- ranging impact of air power, but it also demonstrated its limitations in achieving decisive victory on its own.

The Hollow Force and the Resurgence of Airpower

Exhaustion from over a decade of fighting in Vietnam and the growing budgetary problems resulting from oil prices in the mid-1970s resulted in dramatic defense cuts. The draft ended in 1973, with the All-Volunteer Force becoming the sole basis for recruiting. Recruit quality in the early years was low, in part due to the low public support of the military during the later years of the Vietnam conflict and in part due to gaps in pay and benefits. The pay gap between military and civilian employment grew, peaking at 7.5% in 1979. Budgetary and recruiting strife notwithstanding, the USAF continued fielding new weapons systems. The challenge of sustaining new, technologically advanced aircraft like the F-15, F-16 and A-10 was difficult. Overall mission capable rates dropped to 68% due to a mix of shortages of spare parts and the lack of quality recruits to replace Airmen separating. With the “Reagan Revolution” and ensuing economic recovery, a growing defense budget allowed the USAF to focus on improving sustainment of aircraft and Airmen.

New leadership in the USAF promoted cultures of quality and process improvement. As commander of Tactical Air Command (the predecessor of Air Combat Command) from 1978 to 1984, General Wilbur “Bill” Creech was the pioneer in this effort. Creech instituted policies based on W. Edwards Deming’s philosophy of Total Quality Management into the command’s daily practices, creating a culture of continuous examination and process improvement throughout the USAF that persists to this day in the Continuous Improvement and Innovation program. General Creech also led a transformation of the application of tactical airpower. He led the expansion of Red Flag into a total force concept, introducing night operations, command and control and combat air support activities. The complexity of the exercises expanded from 55 aircraft in 1978 to over 250 in 1984. This reemphasis on the science of tactics, training and multiple components of airpower would bear fruit a few short years later over the sands of Kuwait and Iraq.

p. 77

Operation Desert Shield/Desert Storm

In August 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein ordered an invasion of Kuwait, leading to international condemnation and an economic embargo authorized by the United Nations. In response, President George H.W. Bush initiated Operation DESERT SHIELD, deploying U.S. air and ground units to defend Saudi Arabia and the Persian Gulf states. This marked the largest air deployment in history, surpassing the Berlin Airlift. From August to November 1990, Military Airlift Command (MAC) cargo planes delivered defensive forces, and from November 1990 to January 1991, they brought materials for a counteroffensive. The air bridge covered 7,000 miles and involved 20,500 strategic airlift missions. The operation validated the effectiveness of large-capacity, heavy carriers like the Lockheed C-5A Galaxy and the Lockheed C-141A Starlifter. For the air campaign against Iraq, a planning group known as "Checkmate" developed the plan called INSTANT THUNDER. This four-phase campaign aimed to destroy Iraqi centers of gravity by targeting strategic centers, air defense networks, and ground combat forces. Coalition air forces had to neutralize Iraq's integrated air defense network, which included a large number of combat aircraft, SAMs, and AAA guns.

On January 17, 1991, Operation DESERT STORM began with strikes led by Air Force Special Operations MH-53J PAVE LOW helicopters and Army Apaches. The world witnessed the extensive AAA fire in Iraqi skies, but the stealth capabilities of Lockheed F-117A Nighthawks allowed them to strike heavily defended targets with precision. Under the command of Lt Gen Chuck Horner, 2,700 aircraft executed the master attack plan. During the first week of DESERT STORM, the USAF achieved air supremacy, destroyed the enemy's command and control system, and shot down numerous Iraqi aircraft. The air campaign also involved A-10 Thunderbolt IIs and F-111s targeting armored forces, as well as EF-111A electronic warfare aircraft and intelligence aircraft providing vital support. The DESERT STORM air campaign showcased the dominance of air power on a modern battlefield. Over 44 days, the coalition flew 118,661 sorties, with the U.S. Air Force conducting 60% of them. Precision-guided munitions (PGMs) played a significant role, achieving 80% of known targets destroyed despite accounting for only 8% of the bombs dropped. The effectiveness of the air campaign was not just measured by the destruction of enemy assets but also by its impact on the organizational structure, cohesion of enemy forces, and the psychology of the Iraqi soldier.

The Air Force and Global Positioning

In response to the launch of the Soviet spacecraft Sputnik in 1957, the Air Force began developing a global positioning system (GPS) using satellites. The Navy initially tested satellite systems in the 1960s, but the Air Force had the resources to continue the research. They launched the first NAVSTAR GPS satellite in 1978 and added ten more by 1985. After the Soviet Union shot down Korean Airlines Flight 007 in 1983, the Reagan Administration made GPS technology available to the private sector. The Challenger disaster delayed GPS upgrades until 1989, when operational satellites began deployment. By 1993, the modern GPS constellation was complete with 24 satellites. The system achieved initial operational capability in 1993 and was declared fully operational in 1995 by the Air Force.

p. 78

In the 1990s, the breakup of Yugoslavia presented a significant challenge for NATO. The region faced a long history of conflict, political complexities, and ethnic tensions. As the possibility of a genocidal civil war and destabilization loomed, NATO turned to air power to address the humanitarian crisis and influence events.

In 1999, President Bill Clinton initiated Operation Allied Force, with the primary objectives of demonstrating NATO's opposition to aggression, deterring President Milosevic from further attacks on civilians, and damaging Serbia's war capabilities. Led by Lt Gen General Michael C. Short, NATO air forces conducted over 38,000 sorties from March 24 to June 9, 1999. The campaign aimed to pressure Milosevic, target Serbian forces engaged in Kosovo, and minimize collateral damage and civilian casualties. The air campaign involved 214 strike aircraft in a phased approach against around 50 targets. The Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirit, making its combat debut, delivered 650 Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAMs) in 49 sorties. The scale of the operation grew to involve 563 USAF aircraft and 13,850 American Airmen deployed to 24 locations, resembling a major theater war.

By June 1999, NATO air power achieved its political and military objectives, putting an end to Serbian atrocities, stabilizing Kosovo, and undermining the Milosevic regime. However, there were challenges along the way, including political constraints, adverse weather conditions, and a refugee crisis manufactured by Serbia. Despite efforts to avoid civilian casualties, at least twenty major incidents occurred, including the accidental bombing of the Chinese Embassy.

Overall, the air campaign against Serbia reinforced the effectiveness of air and space power, despite limitations. It highlighted the precision, effectiveness, and speed of these forces. A limited air campaign was seen as the only viable option against an implacable foe. However, the experience also emphasized the costs, risks, and frustrations of gradual air campaigns. It underscored the importance of agreement between air and ground commanders on the enemy's centers of gravity and the need to avoid micromanagement for optimal military effectiveness.

Operation Enduring Freedom and Operation Iraqi Freedom

After the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, the U.S. Air Force played a significant role in the global war on terrorism. Operation ENDURING FREEDOM focused on Afghanistan and involved a coalition of forces, including the Air Force, to combat the Taliban government and Al Qaeda.

Air Force bombers and carrier-strike aircraft conducted military operations, Targeting Taliban air defenses and command centers. They also provided air support to the Afghan Northern Alliance. Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan, fell to coalition forces in November 2001.

Following the success in Afghanistan, President George W. Bush ordered an invasion of Iraq to remove Saddam Hussein from power. Operation IRAQI FREEDOM began in 2003, with the Air Force having gained air superiority over Iraq through previous operations. Coalition air forces conducted a strategic air campaign, targeting enemy command and control systems. Ground forces encountered resistance but were supported by superior training, tactics, and technology, as well as air power. The

p. 79

success of these operations relied on long- term political and economic reconstruction efforts, rather than solely on airpower.

The Air Force also contributed to nation-building activities in Iraq and Afghanistan. This included providing humanitarian aid, civil affairs support, and training Iraqi and Afghan security forces. Joint Air Force-Army Provincial Reconstruction Teams worked on various projects in Afghanistan. The Air Force Academy also played a role in building air forces for Iraq and Afghanistan, with faculty members assisting in training programs and educational initiatives.

Evolution of New Warfighting Domains and Technology

The U.S. Air Force has embraced new technologies such as unmanned vehicles and advancements in the cyber and space domains. The use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) began in 1959 and increased during the Vietnam War. Remotely piloted aircraft took on offensive roles during the Global War on Terror. The Air Force Academy started training cadets in UAV operations in 2010. The Air Force also recognizes the importance of cyberspace and has developed a new cyber strategy to defend against cyberattacks. The Department of War (DoW) has the largest network in the world and must take aggressive steps to secure its data and mitigate risks. In 1982, the Air Force established Air Force Space Command (AFSPC) to focus on space operations. AFSPC expanded its mission to include cyberspace and activated the 24th Air Force for cyberspace operations. The 24th Air Force evolved from a traditional numbered air force into the Air Force's primary cyber warfare organization. Established in 2009, it became Air Forces Cyber (AFCYBER) in 2010 and ultimately merged with the 25th Air Force in 2019 to create the modern 16th Air Force, which now leads the Air Force's information warfare mission.

Operation Inherent Resolve

On October 17, 2014, the Department of War established Combined Joint Task Force Operation INHERENT RESOLVE to coordinate military actions against the threat of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) in Iraq and Syria. This operation involves thirty nations working together to counter the long-term threat posed by ISIL. The mission of CJTF-OIR is threefold: to destroy ISIL military forces, to train and equip regional allies to combat ISIL, and to maximize the effectiveness of coalition contributions to the fight. The United States Air Force has played a critical role in Operation INHERENT RESOLVE through precision strike missions, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance operations, airlift, aerial refueling, and close air support. Since the operation began in 2014, Coalition airpower has enabled the destruction of ISIS's territorial caliphate and continues to support Iraqi and Syrian partner forces in preventing the group's resurgence. Today, the mission focuses on advising and assisting local security forces while conducting targeted operations against remaining ISIS networks in Iraq and Syria. Coalition aircraft conducted more than 34,000 strikes against ISIS targets between 2014 and the defeat of the territorial caliphate.

Creation of the United States Space Force

p. 80

The creation of the United States Space Force was rooted in decades of Air Force space operations under Air Force Space Command (AFSPC), which was established in 1982 to manage military space missions such as satellite operations, missile warning, space surveillance, and GPS. Operation DESERT STORM in 1991 demonstrated the vital importance of space capabilities, leading many to call it the first "space war" because of its reliance on GPS, satellite communications, weather data, and missile warning systems. As space became increasingly contested by potential adversaries, military leaders recognized the need for a dedicated service focused solely on protecting U.S. interests in space. On 20 December 2019, the United States Space Force (USSF) was established as the nation's sixth military branch within the Department of the Air Force. The Space Force organizes, trains, and equips forces to conduct military space operations and protect U.S. and allied space capabilities. Today, the USSF provides critical services including GPS, satellite communications, missile warning, and space domain awareness that enable military operations around the globe.

After the 9/11 attacks, AFSPC provided extensive space-based support to the U.S. Central Command in areas such as communications, positioning, navigation and timing, meteorology, and warning. In 2005, the Air Force expanded AFSPC's mission to include cyberspace operations. The responsibility for conducting cyberspace operations was assigned to AFSPC through the activation of TwentyFourth Air Force in 2009. In 2018, the Air Force transferred the cyber mission to Air Combat Command, allowing AFSPC to focus on gaining and maintaining space superiority and staying ahead of adversaries in the space domain.

Chapter 4Military Strategy

p. 82

National Security Strategy

The national security strategy (NSS) is a document that outlines the United States' overarching approach to protecting its national interests and ensuring its security. The NSS provides a strategic framework for addressing emerging threats, promoting economic prosperity, and advancing American values. The strategy encompasses a wide range of issues, including defense, diplomacy, intelligence, economics, and homeland security, all underpinned with allied efforts when feasible. It guides the government's efforts in formulating policies, allocating resources, and coordinating actions to safeguard the nation's security and promote its global leadership.

National Defense Strategy

The national defense strategy is a document that outlines the United States' approach to national security and defense for civilian and military resources. It provides a strategic framework for the Department of War (DoW) to prioritize its resources, capabilities, and actions to protect the nation's interests. The strategy focuses on addressing emerging threats, such as great power competition, terrorism, cyberattacks, and other challenges to national security. It emphasizes the need for military readiness, innovation, and technological superiority to maintain a credible deterrent and protect American interests at home and abroad. The national defense strategy also emphasizes the importance of alliances and partnerships to strengthen collective security and promote stability. It guides the DoD’s efforts in shaping the force structure, developing capabilities, and conducting military operations to ensure the security and prosperity of the United States.

The National Military Strategy

The United States' national military strategy is a comprehensive plan that outlines how the country's armed forces will be employed to protect and advance its national security interests. It is a key component of the broader national security strategy and provides guidance for the military's role in addressing global challenges. The national military strategy takes into account the evolving threat landscape, geopolitical considerations, and the capabilities of the U.S. military. It outlines strategic objectives, operational concepts, and resource requirements necessary to deter aggression, defend the homeland, and support international security alliances. The strategy also emphasizes the importance of innovation, technological superiority, and interoperability with partner nations to maintain a credible and effective military force.

p. 83

Air Force Operational Imperatives

(https://www.af.mil/Portals/1/documents/2023SAF/OPERATIONAL_ IMPARITIVES_INFOGRAPHIC.pdf )

Secretary of the Air Force, Frank Kendall, released the Operational Imperatives in December 2022. The Air Force operational imperatives are a set of guiding principles that shape the mission and operations of the United States Air Force. These seven imperatives provide a framework for decision-making, strategic planning, and the execution of airpower in support of national security objectives.

1. Space Order of Battle The first operational imperative is to define a resilient and effective space order of battle. More simply stated, this means ensuring resilient space-based capabilities. Both the cyber and physical security of American satellites and sensors must be maintained to ensure operational capability in a future conflict.

2. Operationally Focused Advanced Battle Management System (ABMS)

The ABMS is the Air Force’s contribution to the DoD’s Joint All-Domain Command & Control (JADC2) effort the DoD’s larger concept to connect sensors from all of the military services into a single network. The USAF collects, analyzes, and shares the information needed to make operational decisions at the speed of mission. By incorporating the latest advancements in artificial intelligence, ABMS will revolutionize the speed of battlefield decision-making.

3. Moving Target Engagement The USAF must achieve moving target engagement at scale of a challenging operational environment. Linked to ABMS, this process is especially critical for targets that employ the latest technology designed to evade detection, such as drones, hypersonic weapons or stealth capabilities. This new dimension of warfare necessitates more advanced targeting systems while sensors must be survivable and protected against electromagnetic and cyber attack.

4. Tactical Air Dominance The next generation of air dominance (NGAD) system of systems will be defined by more than the development of 6th-generation fighters, this operational imperative requires the Air Force to integrate crewed aircraft with autonomous aircraft. With NGAD, future crewed aircraft can be accompanied by autonomous wingmen in battle, preserving the lives of pilots without limiting air superiority.

5. Resilient Basing Threats to USAF operations at forward bases can deny U.S. power projection, this imperative is to develop resilient bases and communications. Antiquated method of relying on large, fixed bases, will transition to a “hub-and-spoke” arrangement that incorporates smaller, dispersed, and more mobile bases. This concept is also referred to as Agile Combat Employment (ACE). Smaller mobile bases may complicate logistics but will increase survivability in a combat environment, especially for

p. 84

combat in the Indo-Pacific region.

6. Global Strike Capabilities The USAF is defining the B-21 long-range strike family-of-systems. The B-21 Raider will serve as the backbone of America’s bomber force as a highly adaptable, dual-capable penetrating strike stealth bomber capable of delivering both conventional and nuclear munitions. This multi-functional stealth bomber is designed to handle anything from gathering intelligence, to battle management, to integrating with allies and partners. This operational imperative includes the use of autonomous combat aircraft and other long-range strike aircraft alongside the B-21.

7. Readiness to Deploy and Fight Achieving readiness for a wartime posture against a peer competitor is imperative. Moving forces into theater, and then supporting them takes the collective success of a large number of information systems and supporting logistical and industrial infrastructure. Ensuring the readiness will require effort from the entire USAF and USSF but is instrumental in deterrence.

Air Force Domains

AFH1

Air

Airpower’s exceptional speed and range allow its forces to visit and revisit wide ranges of targets nearly at will. Airpower does not have to occupy terrain or remain constantly in proximity to areas of operation to bring force upon targets.

Space

Global Vigilance, Global Reach, Global Power for America

As the Nation’s space force, the United States Space Force provides critical capabilities that enhance the military’s ability to navigate accurately, see clearly, communicate securely, and strike precisely. Joint, interagency, and coalition forces depend on Space Force operations to perform their missions every day, on every continent, in the air, on the land, and at sea. In a dangerous and uncertain future, the ability to access and exploit space, even when others try to deny us, will be vital to our Nation’s security.

Cyberspace

Cyber operations guarantee our capability to operate in any contested cyber domain to support vital land, sea, air, and space missions by developing capabilities to protect essential military cyber systems and to speed their recovery if an attack does occur. In these interdependent domains the Air Force possesses unique capabilities for ensuring global mobility, long-range strike, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.

Global Vigilance, Global Reach, Global Power for America

Although the way we do them will constantly evolve, the Air Force will continue to perform these missions so that our military can respond quickly and appropriately to unpredictable threats and challenges. Air Force Core Tenets AFDD-1

The application of airpower is refined by several fundamental guiding truths. These truths are known as tenets. They reflect not only the unique historical and doctrinal evolution of airpower, but also the current appreciation for the nature of airpower. The tenets of airpower complement the principles of joint operations. While the principles of war provide general guidance on the application of military forces, the tenets provide more specific considerations for the employment of airpower. The tenets of airpower are:

- Mission Command [Centralized Control & Decentralized Execution].

- Flexibility and Versatility.

- Synergistic Effects.

- Persistence.

- Concentration.

- Priority and Balance Tenets of Airpower

Space Superiority establishes and promotes stable conditions for the safe and secure access to space activities for civil, commercial, intelligence community, and multinational partners.

Combat Power Projection integrates defensive and offensive operations to maintain a desired level of freedom of action relative to an adversary. Combat Power Projection in concert with other competencies enhances freedom of action by deterring aggression or compelling an adversary to change behavior. Principles of War

AFH1

The principles of war are fundamental aspects that tend to lead to military victory. These principles are universally true and relevant throughout the history of conflict. It is important for members of the Air Force to understand how these principles apply to all forces, but particularly to the Air Force. While the complexity and unique nature of each war prevent commanders from using these principles as a checklist for guaranteed victory, they serve as valuable tools to evaluate potential courses of action. The principles of war are interconnected and should be considered together. They are not exhaustive, but rather provide a framework for developing strategies and doctrines for the Air Force. Airmen must be able to view these principles from a three-dimensional perspective and integrate them accordingly. When combined with the tenets of AirPower, the principles of war provide a solid foundation for the air, space, and cyber forces of the joint force in America.

Unity of Command – concentration of effort for every objective responsible commander. Objective – direct military operations toward a defined and attainable objective that contributes to strategic, operational, and tactical aims.

Mass – concentrate the effects of combat power at the most advantageous place and time to achieve decisive results.

Maneuver – place the enemy in a position of disadvantage through the flexible application of combat power.

Surprise – attacking the enemy at a time, place, or in a manner for which they are not prepared.

Simplicity – avoid unnecessary complexity in organizing, preparing, planning, and conducting military operations.

Economy of Force – judicious employment and distribution of forces

p. 88

Security – never permit the enemy to acquire unexpected advantage.

Offensive – seize, retain, and exploit the initiative.

Department of the Air Force AFDD-1

The Air Force employs air, space, and cyberspace capabilities with a broader focus on theater-wide and national-level objectives. Through airpower, the Air Force provides the versatile, wide-ranging means towards achieving national objectives with the ability to deter and respond immediately to crises anywhere in the world. It includes all elements and units of the United States Air Force (USAF) and the United States Space Force (USSF). The USSF was established December 20, 2019, and is the space operations service branch.

U.S. Air Force Mission

The mission of the United States Air Force is to fly, fight and win - airpower anytime, anywhere.

U.S. Space Force Mission

Secure our Nation's interest in, from and to space.

p. 90

Department of the Army ADP-1

U.S. forces operate in the air, land, maritime, space, and cyberspace domains. The land domain is the most complex of the domains, because it addresses humanity — its cultures, ethnicities, religions, and politics. War begins and ends based upon how it affects the land domain. Air, maritime, space, and cybernetic power affect the land domain indirectly; landpower is usually the arbiter of victory. The Army provides the United States with the landpower to prevent, shape, and win in the land domain. U.S. law, Department of War directives, and the nature of landpower mold the Army’s mission.

U.S. Army Mission

The Mission of the United States army is to fight and win our Nation’s wars, by providing prompt, sustained, land dominance, across the full range of military operations and the spectrum of conflict, in support of combatant commanders.

Department of the Navy NDP-1

The job of gaining and maintaining maritime superiority or supremacy of engaging in and winning battles in the maritime domain and preventing conflict through presence offshore falls almost exclusively to the Naval Service. The Naval Service comprises the Active and Reserve components and the civilian personnel of the United States Navy, the United States Marine Corps, and the United States Coast Guard. Note: The United States Coast Guard falls under the Department of Homeland Security as a peacetime law enforcement agency.

U.S. Navy Mission

The mission of the Navy is to maintain, train and equip combat-ready Naval forces capable of winning wars, deterring aggression and maintaining freedom of the seas.

Marine Corp Vision

The Marine Corps plays an integral role in the National Defense Strategy. Its training, capabilities and global presence ensure that the Navy-Marine Corps team remains an expeditionary force-in-readiness when responding to crises, creating decision space or winning battles.

p. 91

USAFE-Air Force Africa directs air operations in a theater. Spanning three continents, covering more than 15 million square miles, containing 104 independent states, and possessing more than one-fifth of the world’s population and more than a quarter of the world’s gross domestic product.
